clue.text: Beat a saint, or train a priest here in Dyfed

definitions.text: train a priest here in Dyfed

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or beat someone
Peter is the apostle and saint

explanation.surface: Someone in Wales weighs up thrashing a saint or training for the priesthood.
explanation.walkthrough: LAMPETER is a small university town in west Wales (Dyfed was the county) whose St David's College long trained Anglican clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: The town's college was founded to educate Welsh ordinands, so it is the Dyfed place where a cleric was trained.

clue.text: A duck in Nature's evolution becomes a flier

indicators.note: the zero goes inside the rearranged letters
evolution means gradual change, so the letters develop into a new order

parts.note: the word nature with its possessive giving no letter
a duck is a zero score in cricket, O

explanation.surface: A duck evolves into a creature of the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evolution' rearranges NATURE into ERNAUT, and 'in' puts O inside it to make ERONAUT, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: A balloonist or airship traveller is someone who flies.

clue.text: Absurd appearance before and after use or otherwise

parts.note: pre is the prefix meaning before
post is the prefix meaning after

indicators.note: otherwise means in a different way, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ridiculous appearance before and after use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' scrambles USE OR into EROUS; 'appearance' is a link word. The word literally means before-after, the wrong way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Something utterly contrary to reason or sense is ridiculous.

clue.text: Little sign of lamenting rent fall?

parts.note: a rent is a rip or tear
a drop is a fall

explanation.surface: Someone sheds a tear over a fall in rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like money paid for housing, but it is a rip.
explanation.definitionFit: A single shed drop of crying is a small sign of grief.

clue.text: Dory-man confounded him

indicators.note: confounded means mixed up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A fisherman in a small boat baffled some fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: A dory is a small flat-bottomed fishing boat. The definition is just 'him': a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, so a male person can be referred to as this.

clue.text: French maid with West End headwear

parts.note: bonne is French for a maid or nursemaid

indicators.note: the end of the word West is its final letter

explanation.surface: A French maid in the West End wears a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The West End is London's theatre district, but here it means the last letter of 'West'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hat tied under the chin is a classic women's head covering.

clue.text: Mount seen going through Trossachs

indicators.note: the mountain's name runs through the middle of the place name

explanation.surface: A mountain is seen on a drive through Scottish hill country.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trossachs are a wooded glen area in Scotland; Ossa is a mountain in Greece (piled on Pelion in myth).
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a peak in Thessaly, Greece, a mountain.

clue.text: Perhaps property managers get letters written about corrosion

indicators.note: the spelt letters are written around the corrosion

parts.note: the letter T spelt out twice gives tees, letters
rust is corrosion

explanation.surface: Estate agents receive letters complaining about rust.
explanation.walkthrough: TEES is the plural of the letter T spelt out, as in 'letters'.
explanation.definitionFit: People holding property on behalf of others manage it, an example of such managers.

clue.text: Spray — a tiny bit is seen by East River

parts.note: an atom is a minute particle
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fine mist drifts beside a river on its eastern bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A scent spray is a device that turns liquid into a fine mist.

clue.text: Bare sort of hillside

indicators.note: a sort of the word means a rearranged version of its letters here

explanation.surface: A treeless slope on a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: BRAE is the Scots word for a hillside or slope.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots and northern English use the word for the slope of a hill.

clue.text: Luggage left with someone — given a drink by us

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
man stands for a person, someone
tea is a drink
taken as written

explanation.surface: A traveller hands their bags to a porter who is then offered a cuppa.
explanation.definitionFit: These are large travelling trunks that open into two halves, a type of baggage.

clue.text: Work of reference — I need a copy — £100 outlay

indicators.note: outlay is read as laid out, setting the letters in a new order

parts.note: the pound sign is L, from libra, and 100 is the Roman numeral C

explanation.surface: A researcher must spend a hundred pounds on a copy of a reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outlay' rearranges I NEED A COPY plus C and L.
explanation.definitionFit: A multi-volume book of general knowledge is a standard reference work.

clue.text: Person contemplating carrying a German rifle?

indicators.note: the pondering person holds the next letter inside, as one carries a load

parts.note: a muser is someone who muses or ponders

explanation.surface: A thoughtful soldier walks along with a German gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mauser company of Germany made famous bolt-action rifles, so the maker's name stands for the gun.

clue.text: Seen coat we mislaid? May be money in it

indicators.note: something mislaid is put in the wrong place, so the letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A lost coat may have had cash in its pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we mislaid' tells you to scramble SEEN COAT. NOTE-CASE is an old word for a wallet for banknotes.
explanation.definitionFit: A wallet for banknotes is the kind of thing that may hold cash.

clue.text: Must be made to try

parts.note: the stock phrase that one of these must be made, combined with a bid to try, describes an effort

explanation.surface: Someone is ordered to have a go at something.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on the set phrase 'an effort must be made': the answer is a try, and it is what must be made.
explanation.definitionFit: A try or go at something is an effort made, and the noun is what one says must be made.

clue.text: Frightening news for Capone's enemies ?

definitions.meaning: Al Capone's enemies would hear that Al is taking up weapons

explanation.walkthrough: Split as AL ARMING: Al Capone is gearing up with guns, which is scary news for his rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scary or disturbing is worrying, and Al getting armed would scare his foes.

clue.text: Thousands round the racecourse, lucky things!

indicators.note: the thousands are placed around the course name

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so two of them is MS
Ascot is the famous racecourse in Berkshire

explanation.surface: Crowds of thousands around a racecourse cheer their good luck charms.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a well-known English racecourse, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Charms or creatures kept to bring good luck are emblems of fortune.

clue.text: Tales feature the customary drawings ?

definitions.meaning: bank records routinely show withdrawals of money, the drawings

explanation.walkthrough: 'drawings' looks like pictures, but means money drawn from a bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Narratives are reports or stories, and bank records list cash withdrawals.

clue.text: 2's panic ends quietly at home

parts.note: tails are ends
p is piano, the musical direction for quietly
in means at home

explanation.surface: A flier's terror ends calmly back at home.
explanation.walkthrough: '2's' refers to the answer of 2 down, an aerial flier: a spinning dive of an aircraft is a pilot's emergency, and figuratively any panic.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep spiralling dive out of control is the airman's nightmare, and by extension a state of chaos.

clue.text: A number object to be in parliament

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
a thing is an object

explanation.surface: Someone is told a certain item is to go before parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The ALTHING is the parliament of Iceland, one of the oldest in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Iceland's national assembly is its legislature.

clue.text: Unusual for Jack to take girl money

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, an able seaman, AB
Norma is a girl's name
L stands for pound, as in the £ sign from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A sailor is odd to take a girl's cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Something out of the ordinary is irregular or strange.

clue.text: Natives have choice of vowels in writing

indicators.note: the vowel choice sits inside the writing

parts.note: MS is manuscript, a piece of writing
a choice between vowels is A or I

explanation.surface: Indigenous people choose vowels when they write.
explanation.walkthrough: The Maori are the indigenous people of New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Polynesian people of New Zealand are its first inhabitants.

clue.text: Eastern labourer of low degree? That's the answer

parts.note: a low degree of temperature is cool
i.e., Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A humble worker from the East is presented as the solution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the answer' is a link phrase. The word is now regarded as an offensive term for an Asian manual labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: The historical term named an unskilled hired worker in India or China.

clue.text: Union has some members in official London residence

indicators.note: the fodder's letters are taken as members to be reorganised in a new body

explanation.surface: Union delegates gather at a Lord Mayor's grand home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'members in' signals scrambling the twelve letters of UNION HAS SOME. The Mansion House is the Lord Mayor of London's official residence.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lord Mayor of the City of London lives in this grand eighteenth-century building.

clue.text: Crazy May gatherings ?

definitions.meaning: from the rhyme 'Here we go gathering ... in May'

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Here we go gathering nuts in May' gives the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for mad, and the things gathered in the children's rhyme.

clue.text: The Sun's rim —: the stars rush out" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: The Sun's rim —: the stars rush out" (Coleridge)

parts.words: The Sun's rim —: the stars rush out" (Coleridge)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, where the sun sinks below the horizon

explanation.surface: A line of Romantic poetry about sunset with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Coleridge's Ancient Mariner is 'The Sun's rim dips; the stars rush out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb describes the sun sinking or going down below the horizon.

clue.text: People read about O.T. system of symbols

indicators.note: the word for people is placed around the abbreviation

parts.note: a nation is a people
taken as written, the letters of the abbreviation

explanation.surface: Readers of the Old Testament pore over a scriptural code.
explanation.definitionFit: Written signs used for music, mathematics or chess form such a code of symbols.

clue.text: Chief corridors of power for sophistical rhetoricians ? .

definitions.text: Chief corridors of power for sophistical rhetoricians ? .

parts.words: Chief corridors of power for sophistical rhetoricians
parts.note: main channels carrying fuel are read as the leading conduits of empty talk for windbags

explanation.surface: Smooth-talking orators prowl the main corridors of government.
explanation.walkthrough: Gas is empty talk, the windbag rhetorician's power; the main pipes carrying the fuel are its chief corridors.
explanation.definitionFit: Principal pipelines carrying fuel gas are conduits of power, and gas is also windy talk.
